newsitem.title: USA: IRS memo not likely to boost 1996 farm taxes.
newsitem.headline: IRS memo not likely to boost 1996 farm taxes.

text.p: Farmers need not worry that a 1995 Internal Revenue Service memo could boost taxes on 1996 cash grain deals, grain industry sources said Thursday.
"Yes, it (the memo) is a possible problem. But it should not be blown out of proportion," said David Barrett of the National Grain and Feed Association.
At issue is a December 1995 IRS memo about a Washington state farmer who sold potatoes and received some cash at delivery but deferred some payment until the following year.
In that case, IRS ruled that the entire income from the sale must be reported under alternative minimum tax rules, applicable for the same tax year.
The alternative minimum tax covers a broader base of income at a lower rate. A farmer must pay the alternative minimum tax if it exceeds normal income tax.
With trade publications buzzing about the threat, grain farmers are pondering whether to avoid deferred payments and store grain until next year.
But tax experts said the memo does not cover traditional deferred payments grain contracts, which typically do not involve up-front payments prior to Jan. 1.
"It's not clear that simple DP (deferred payment) contracts are subject to AMT (alternative minimum tax)," said Dave Miller, commodity policy specialist at the American Farm Bureau Federation.

To avoid problems, farmers should sign contracts citing delivery and payment dates and proving no money changed hands at the time of delivery, said Tom Husek, accountant with the Illinois Agricultural Auditing Association.
Husek also noted that the IRS memo has not been officially approved or published in the National Register and probably would not be approved in time to affect 1996 taxes.
An IRS spokeswoman in Washington told Reuters on Monday the memo applies only to the case of the Washington farmer.
